{"id": "26:181/q09", "question": "What harm or moral principle explains the ban on cheating?", "turns_on": "The notes stress different, compatible grounds: spiritual damage, violation of property rights, or wider economic and social harm.", "positions": [{"id": "26:181/q09/p1", "position": "Greed and neglect of God lead to cheating, which damages one's religion.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī identifies greed for money as the underlying problem and says shortchanging others impoverishes one's religion, though a passing impulse can be resisted. Iṣlāḥī says Midian's traders became open to Satan's distortion of trade when they grew indifferent to God and the Hereafter."}, {"id": "26:181/q09/p2", "position": "Short measurement oppresses buyers and amounts to illicit taking of their property.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr names short measure and weight as oppression and illicit consumption, compounded by merchants' collusion that forced buyers into these dealings. Al-Qurṭubī requires just weighing and delivery of people's due."}, {"id": "26:181/q09/p3", "position": "Fraud spreads among traders, widening exploitation and threatening society's economic balance.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī calls fraudulent weighing a contagious economic disease drawing traders and businesses into broader deception. He says God's ordering of the world by balance guides justice across society and the economy, whose balance can collapse."}]}
{"id": "26:181/q10", "question": "How does this injunction fit the surrounding prophetic narratives?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "26:181/q10/p1", "position": "Shuayb turns from the general call to worship to detailed rules for transactions.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links the turn to the earlier call at 26:177 and to his people's shirk, cheating, undervaluing of goods, and corruption."}, {"id": "26:181/q10/p2", "position": "The messengers' shared message is piety, obedience, exclusive worship, and no demand for payment.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī explains the repeated prophetic answer through these common demands."}, {"id": "26:181/q10/p3", "position": "Shuayb's warning against economic misconduct parallels Lot's warning against moral misconduct and ends with the familiar fate and repeated verses.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī identifies Shuayb's people here as Midian and places their persistence, destruction, and the closing repeated verses in the sūra's pattern of nations."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q01", "question": "What does qaḍā al-ajal say Moses completed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q01/p1", "position": "He fulfilled the agreed period of service and its work.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies the agreement with the father-in-law who gave his daughter in marriage; al-Biqāʿī says Moses fulfilled all promised work. Al-Ālūsī treats the opening fāʾ as resuming the sequence of contract, work, completion, and departure. Al-Dāmghānī gives completion of a term as one sense of qaḍā, alongside completion of revelation."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q02", "question": "How long did Moses fulfill or remain after his contract?", "turns_on": "The reports give ten or twenty years; some authors judge the extra decade weak, while others stress that the verse itself does not specify eight versus ten.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q02/p1", "position": "He fulfilled the longer, better term of ten years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās argues prophets keep promises, eight years were binding, and God fulfills the fuller promise; Saʿīd's Jewish questioner accepted this answer. Reports attribute the answer to the Prophet directly, via Gabriel or a higher angel, or to God after successive consultations. Al-Ṭabarī's reports variously call it the last, fullest, most virtuous, or most honored term. Al-Ālūsī cites Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bukhārī transmissions; Elmalılı reasons a noble person does not leave a promise incomplete."}, {"id": "28:29/q02/p2", "position": "He served ten years, then remained a further ten, leaving after twenty.", "reasons": "Mujāhid supplies the additional decade in numerous transmissions. Al-Bayḍāwī reports it with his summary; al-Biqāʿī infers some interval because 'and he traveled' is coordinated rather than a direct result. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the twenty-year report weak, as do Abū Ḥayyān and his source cited by al-Qurṭubī; Ibn Kathīr has not found other support beyond Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim."}, {"id": "28:29/q02/p3", "position": "He stayed additional unspecified years after taking his wife.", "reasons": "Wahb ibn Munabbih reports years beyond the marriage without giving a number."}, {"id": "28:29/q02/p4", "position": "The verse and Torah do not settle whether the service was eight or ten years.", "reasons": "Islāḥī states both texts leave the term unspecified; Kuran Yolu likewise distinguishes the Qur'an's silence from exegetical ten-year reports."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q03", "question": "What happened to the flock given to Moses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q03/p1", "position": "A promised share of differently colored newborn lambs multiplied after Moses used a device at the water.", "reasons": "Anas describes a reflection at the water and nearly all lambs born piebald. The report through ʿUtba says Moses served for chastity and food, placed his staff at the trough, and received multiplied varied-color newborns. Ibn Lahiʿa also defines five livestock types named in this account: abundant-milk fashūsh, long-udder tanūb, low-yield ʿazūz, two-nub thaʿūl, and small-udder kamsha."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q04", "question": "Which daughter did Moses marry?", "turns_on": "Conflicting reports identify the bride as elder or younger; one source conditions following the Prophetic younger-daughter report on its soundness.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q04/p1", "position": "He married the younger daughter.", "reasons": "Reports attribute this to the Prophet; al-Thaʿlabī says the report must be followed if sound. Al-Wāḥidī transmits Gabriel's instruction to say it; al-Ṭabrisī identifies her as the one who urged her father to hire Moses. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī note conflict with another account."}, {"id": "28:29/q04/p2", "position": "He married the elder daughter.", "reasons": "Wahb supplies this report. Abū Ḥayyān notes exegetical disagreement also over her name."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q05", "question": "Where did Moses travel after the term?", "turns_on": "Whether the destination was Egypt to revisit kin or Jerusalem/Syria; Elmalılı cites 28:33 against Egypt, while al-Ālūsī finds Egypt likelier.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q05/p1", "position": "He headed toward Egypt, his homeland and relatives.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls Egypt his home; al-Baghawī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān likewise identify it. Mujāhid says he sought permission to visit his mother and brother. Ibn Kathīr adds longing for family and secret travel because of Pharaoh. Al-Ālūsī says Moses thought the old affair forgotten and judges Jerusalem less likely; Elmalılı objects that Egypt conflicts with Moses' earlier fear of being killed at 28:33."}, {"id": "28:29/q05/p2", "position": "He headed toward Syria or Jerusalem.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives Syria in the narrative ellipsis and Abū Baṣīr reports Jerusalem. Elmalılı prefers Jerusalem as safer and more fitting; al-Ālūsī reports it but regards it as less likely. Islāḥī describes the mount destination without fixing Egypt."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q06", "question": "What does sāra imply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q06/p1", "position": "It means to travel through the land, especially sustained movement toward a purpose or destination.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī groups uses at 40:21 and 6:11; Būrsawī defines motion through land. Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes purposive extended travel from mere walking, citing 6:11 and 25:63."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q07", "question": "Who accompanied Moses as his family?", "turns_on": "The plural household is variously expanded beyond the wife, and accounts disagree when a child was born.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q07/p1", "position": "His wife accompanied him.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī states the minimal identification; other reports add companions. Kashīfī, as cited by Būrsawī, treats the bāʾ as causative, 'he took his family.' Ibn al-Jawzī's Nuzha reports some exegetes using this very journey as an example in which ahl refers to a wife."}, {"id": "28:29/q07/p2", "position": "His wife and child or children accompanied him.", "reasons": "Muqātil adds a flock. Kashf al-Asrār names his wife Ṣafūriyya and a child born before departure. Al-Ālūsī reports two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, requiring extra years if marriage was consummated only after the contract. Islāḥī says the Torah gives wife and two children. Al-Dāmghānī gives wife and children as a lexical sense of ahl, also mentioning 27:57."}, {"id": "28:29/q07/p3", "position": "His wife and a servant accompanied him.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as one identification of the household."}, {"id": "28:29/q07/p4", "position": "A child was born during the journey on the night of the fire.", "reasons": "Wahb supplies this alternative timing of the child's birth."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q08", "question": "What hardships marked the journey and sighting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q08/p1", "position": "They traveled on a dark, cold winter night, lost the route, and had trouble making fire.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī say they lost the road; Mujāhid says Moses avoided Syrian rulers, his wife was pregnant or in labor, and his flint failed. Al-Naqqāsh adds Friday, a divine light in a tree, lost fire, and severe cold. Other accounts add rain, snow, scattered sheep, alternating caravan travel, and a remote flame; some place it on the mount's western right side. Al-Biqāʿī infers winter from their need to warm themselves."}]}

 [{"id": "28:29/q09/p1", "position": "They waited while Moses went to the fire.", "reasons": "Būrsawī says Moses left them and went to the fire before the call came from the right bank."}, {"id": "28:29/q09/p2", "position": "His wife, child, and flock were left in the wilderness for thirty years.", "reasons": "Muqātil says a shepherd eventually found her and returned her to her father."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q10", "question": "What does al-Ṭūr refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the term is treated as the specific Sinai mount or a general mountain word in Arabic.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q10/p1", "position": "It is Mount Sinai, a particular known mountain.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya locates it in Syria and says ṭūr may mean any mountain, though some restrict it to a bare mountain. Asad consistently translates it Mount Sinai because he takes the Qur'anic term to refer invariably to it. Būrsawī identifies the definite form as a particular mountain."}, {"id": "28:29/q10/p2", "position": "It means a mountain generally, with a possible restriction to one without vegetation.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā glosses ṭūr simply as mountain; Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies the broader usage and the bare-mountain qualification."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q11", "question": "Where was the fire in relation to Moses and the mount?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q11/p1", "position": "It appeared from the mount's side, described as the right or western side from Moses' viewpoint.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and Būrsawī take jānib as the side facing him. Ibn Kathīr places it to Moses' right when facing the qiblah, on the western side near the valley's green tree. Mujāhid's report likewise calls it the western right side. Būrsawī locates the subsequent call at the right bank relative to Moses, a watercourse between mountains."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q12", "question": "What does ānasa mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether īnās is simple visual perception or carries familiarity and comfort.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q12/p1", "position": "He perceived or saw the fire, especially by sight.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites al-Aʿshāʿj's line about spotting a bird near the mountain; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adduces 4:6 and Ḥassān's line. Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Azharī's idiom of looking for anyone present and al-Nābigha's watchful bull. Al-Ālūsī says perception is the broader original sense and reports al-Zamakhsharī's clear, unambiguous sight; al-Māwardī includes knowing."}, {"id": "28:29/q12/p2", "position": "He perceived something familiar, intimate, or reassuring.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī stresses reassurance. Būrsawī says the light cheered him; Elmalılı links a humanly intimate perception to recognizing maturity at 4:6. Al-Ālūsī reports this as a distinct nuance. Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir reads it inwardly as familiarity with the pure site and divine conversation."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q13", "question": "What was the fire Moses saw?", "turns_on": "Whether the apparent fire was light, fire, or fire with a reality beyond ordinary perception.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q13/p1", "position": "It was divine light appearing to Moses as fire.", "reasons": "Qatāda says it only seemed fire; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it God's light. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ and Jaʿfar describe prophetic and sacred lights. Būrsawī says light appeared dressed as fire to meet Moses' wintry need, comparing Gabriel's familiar appearance as Diḥya. Al-Ālūsī reports mystics calling it real light misnamed fire; al-Qushayrī says God showed fire, then light, to lead Moses to hearing Him."}, {"id": "28:29/q13/p2", "position": "It appeared as actual fire on the mountain, though its reality exceeded ordinary reason.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī and other narrative reports describe seeing fire on the mount. Al-Ālūsī transmits a mystical view that its appearance was actual fire while its reality surpassed reason."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q14", "question": "What tree is associated with the fire and call?", "turns_on": "Reports name different tree species; Ibn Kathīr grades the samurah report's chain fair.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q14/p1", "position": "It was an acacia or samurah tree.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd calls it a fresh green samurah; Ibn Kathīr rates that chain fair. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also transmits an acacia identification from Ibn Masʿūd."}, {"id": "28:29/q14/p2", "position": "It was an oleander.", "reasons": "Wahb is named for this identification by Ibn ʿAṭiyya."}, {"id": "28:29/q14/p3", "position": "It was hawthorn or azarole.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes hawthorn to Qatāda and notes another report of azarole."}, {"id": "28:29/q14/p4", "position": "It was an ʿullayq or ʿawsaj bush.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits ʿullayq from Wahb and ʿawsaj from some People of the Book."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q15", "question": "What does the indefinite nāran suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q15/p1", "position": "It signals a strange, wondrous or unlikely fire.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reads wonder in the indefinite tanwīn; al-Biqāʿī says Moses' emphatic claim of seeing fire responds to the improbability of a flame in a remote cold place."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q16", "question": "Who says 'wait' and what does amkuthū mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q16/p1", "position": "Moses told his family to remain in place while he went toward the fire.", "reasons": "Būrsawī explicitly identifies Moses as speaker and glosses amkuthū as staying and waiting."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q17", "question": "Why is the command to the family plural and masculine?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q17/p1", "position": "The plural indicates several companions; masculine agreement follows precedence or includes sons.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the plural establishes more than one companion. Al-Biqāʿī invokes grammatical masculine precedence, possible sons, and the need to shelter women."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q18", "question": "What news did Moses hope to obtain?", "turns_on": "Whether khabar concerns the lost route or whether the fire itself offers welcome or danger.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q18/p1", "position": "Directions or information about the road and destination.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, Ibn ʿAbbās and many commentators say the party was lost and Moses expected people by the fire. Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī specify whether the route was straight or diverted; Būrsawī specifies Egypt. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses the parallel 20:10 as stronger evidence. Asad treats 'about which route to take' as ellipsis; al-Zajjāj says he wanted to know why the fire was lit."}, {"id": "28:29/q18/p2", "position": "He sought to learn whether the fire signaled comfort or danger.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī give this as an alternative to route information."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q19", "question": "Why call the hoped-for information khabar?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q19/p1", "position": "Khabar is ordinary news; nabaʾ carries greater importance and benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī's linguists distinguish the two; he derives nabaʾ from emergence and observes singular khabar twice in Moses' story, against nabaʾ for weighty accounts of earlier peoples and messengers at 27:22, 38:67, 78:2, 64:5, 14:9, 10:71, and 11:120."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q20", "question": "What does jadhwah denote?", "turns_on": "The lexical range runs from a thick log without flame through burning wood to flame or ember itself; poetry and reports support different restrictions.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q20/p1", "position": "A substantial piece of wood or log, with or without fire.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda compares jadhwah with jadhmah, a thick log; al-Zajjāj and al-Mubarrad agree. Ibn Muqbil's jadhā and Kuthayyir's verse attest large firewood; al-Samīn notes the poem about nonflaring logs but also a poem describing a blaze. Ibn ʿAṭiyya suggests roots used as desert fuel, citing al-Sulamī's smoking-roots line. Al-Rāghib and al-Mufradāt describe wood left after burning; the plural appears as jadhā or judhiyy. Al-Kashshāf allows fire at its end or none, while this context calls for a usable burning piece. Abū Ḥayyān explains Ibn Muqbil's poetic contrast: khawār breaks apart and dhaʿr is worn wood, unlike the large sturdy fuel. He reports al-Sulamī defining the thick stick as burning or unburning and citing al-Sulamī's verse in which al-jadhā denotes firewood amid an old man's hardship."}, {"id": "28:29/q20/p2", "position": "A piece, stump, root or branch of wood containing fire, sometimes without a flame.", "reasons": "Qatāda specifies a tree base with fire at the tip, Mujāhid its base, al-Kalbī a partly burned stick, and Ibn Zayd fire within wood. Reports vary between burning end, partly burned stick, glowing coal and ember. Al-Samīn says this context requires a burning piece; al-Ālūsī says min al-nār clarifies it. Qatāda links it to winter warmth. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Farrāʾ deriving jadhwah from cutting off and defining it as wood containing fire without flame."}, {"id": "28:29/q20/p3", "position": "A flame, meteor, or glowing firebrand itself.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī speaks of a flame; Ibn ʿAbbās uses meteor, ember, or flaming brand in different reports. Al-Kashshāf cites an anonymous poem of a blazing brand. Al-Samarrāʾī calls it an ember or piece of fire; Elmalılı renders it Turkish 'eksi'. Abū Ḥayyān cites an unnamed poet using jadhwah for an ember taken from a fire and describing its remaining heat and blaze."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q21", "question": "How is the jīm of jadhwah read?", "turns_on": "Three Arabic dialect vowelings of the first radical; kasra is most widespread and explicitly preferred by two lexicographic commentators.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q21/p1", "position": "With kasra, jidhwah.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī are named among its readers; al-Ṭabarī prefers the best-known Ḥijāzī, Baṣran and some Kūfan form without rejecting fatḥa. Ibn Khālawayh calls kasra most eloquent. The forms are dialectal, and Qiraat-ER notes a

Ibn al-Jazarī's Nashr assigns kasra to the remaining readers after naming the fatḥa and ḍamma groups."}, {"id": "28:29/q21/p2", "position": "With fatḥa, jadhwah.", "reasons": "ʿĀṣim is the main named reader; al-Qurṭubī also names al-Sulamī and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, and Abū Ḥayyān excepts al-Jaʿfī from ʿĀṣim. Al-Ṭabarī accepts the less common form. Ibn Mujāhid and Ibn al-Jazarī both name ʿĀṣim for fatḥa; Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Sulamī's recognition of all three initial vowels."}, {"id": "28:29/q21/p3", "position": "With ḍamma, judhwah.", "reasons": "Ḥamza is the main named reader, with al-Aʿmash, Ṭalḥa and Abū Ḥaywa also reported; Ibn al-Jawzī adds Khalaf and al-Walīd from Ibn ʿĀmir, while al-Qurṭubī names Yaḥyā. Qiraat-ER notes dictionaries attest all three vowels. Ibn Mujāhid names Ḥamza for ḍamma; Ibn al-Jazarī adds Khalaf. Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Sulamī's recognition of all three initial vowels."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q22", "question": "How does min al-nār attach and function?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q22/p1", "position": "It qualifies jadhwah and marks the source of the burning piece.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn attaches the phrase to jadhwah rather than ātīkum, saying this fire is not simply the first-mentioned fire and Arabic may repeat a noun with a pronoun or definite article. Al-Ālūsī, citing Qatāda's burning tree base, takes min as source from the fire Moses had noticed."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q23", "question": "What does taṣṭalūn mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q23/p1", "position": "To warm yourselves or shelter from cold by fire.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya traces it to ṣalā, the heat of fire, with tāʾ changed to ṭāʾ. Būrsawī notes variant forms of the noun ṣalāʾ. Reports tie the purpose to the winter cold; al-Biqāʿī says they might draw near the fire."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q24", "question": "What would Moses do if he found no news?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q24/p1", "position": "He would bring back a burning branch or ember for warmth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās sets the firebrand as the fallback if no information emerged. Al-Ṭabarī compares 20:10; other commentators stress the two immediate needs, guidance and warmth."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q25", "question": "Why does Moses say laʿallī and laʿallakum?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q25/p1", "position": "They express hope and humility amid uncertainty.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī relates tentative speech to the sūra's theme of humility; al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts hopeful laʿallī in al-Qaṣaṣ with future sīn and resolve in al-Naml, saying circumstances may let speakers move between commitment and hope without contradiction. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says Moses' fear in al-Qaṣaṣ makes his promised news tentative, while al-Naml's confident wording fits its less fearful scene; a blazing brand is harder to bring than an ember. He counts ten expressions of hope in al-Qaṣaṣ but only two in al-Naml, making hope a recurring feature of this sūra."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q26", "question": "How does this wording compare with the fire scene in al-Naml?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q26/p1", "position": "Al-Qaṣaṣ uses hope, one 'come,' and a possible ember to fit a fearful scene; al-Naml uses certainty, repeated coming, and a bright flame for strength.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī links al-Qaṣaṣ's fear back before Moses' birth and al-Naml's future sīn and repetition to empowerment; atā occurs twelve times in al-Naml and six in al-Qaṣaṣ. A shihāb is a bright flame, qabas a flame taken from a larger fire and also a root for acquiring knowledge; it brings more light and warmth than a jadhwah, which may lack flame. His lecture notes say al-Qaṣaṣ only promises a possible ember, not expressly taking it from the fire, and that each wording accurately suits its context. Al-Sāmarrāʾī adds that al-Qaṣaṣ locates the fire at the mountain's side and gives Moses' instruction to wait because its telling develops the scene more fully, whereas al-Naml is concise. He pairs the more specific idkhāl with shihāb qabas and the broader sulūk with jadhwah; a blazing brand is harder to bring than an ember. He also counts ten expressions of hope in al-Qaṣaṣ against two in al-Naml, fitting their tentative and confident promises respectively."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q27", "question": "What other textual links are made to this scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q27/p1", "position": "The fire episode recurs or is explained at 20:9–10, 27:7–8 and elsewhere.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān and Asad point to earlier discussions; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses 20:10 for guidance. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Qur'an adds the mountain fire to Exodus's journey account. Study Quran also names 26:10; its introduction continues from the fire to God's speech, miracles, and Aaron's help at 28:30–35. {"id": "28:29/q36", "question": "What readings and word derivations are noted for the later signs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q36/p1", "position": "Al-buqʿah, rahb and dhānika have reported variant vocalizations.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī gives ḍamma or fatḥa for buqʿah, four vowel patterns for rahb meaning fear, and light dual dhānika from dhāka versus doubled dual from dhālika."}, {"id": "28:29/q36/p2", "position": "Burhān and sulṭān name illuminating proof.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī derives burhān's brightness from a fair woman's description, treats n as extra by comparison with abraha, and links sulṭān to salīṭ, oil, because proof gives light."}]}
{"id": "28:29/q37", "question": "How does the Torah account of Moses before the fire relate to the Qur'anic account?", "turns_on": "Whether specific Torah details can be reconciled with Qur'anic narration or indicate textual alteration.", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q37/p1", "position": "The Torah recounts Israel's oppression, Moses' rescue and flight, and his Midian marriage; details differ from the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī quotes Jacob's seventy descendants in Egypt, Pharaoh's forced labor and infanticide, midwives Puah and Shiphrah, Moses' basket, Pharaoh's daughter and naming, his killing of an Egyptian, escape, Reuel's seven daughters, marriage to Zipporah and son Eliezer. {"id": "28:29/q41", "question": "What virtues or protection are reported for reciting and carrying the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:29/q41/p1", "position": "The Qur'an protects, intercedes and rewards those who recite and practice it.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī cites Ibn al-Anbārī and reports through ʿIṣma and Sahl likening its immunity from Fire to a hide containing Qur'an; Anas says faithful readers are protected, aided at Judgment and among Paradise's notables and God's elect. {"id": "29:57/q06", "question": "How is 'tasting death' read and constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether dhāʾiqa governs al-mawt as a construct or is nunated and takes an accusative object.", "positions": [{"id": "29:57/q06/p1", "position": "Dhāʾiqat al-mawt is read as a genitive construction.", "reasons": "Jishumi states the construct reading and allows another construction; his separate note about ka-ʾayyin glosses that neighboring word as 'how many.'"}, {"id": "29:57/q06/p2", "position": "Dhāʾiqatun al-mawta is read with nunation and accusative 'death'.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Alusi attribute this reading to Abu Haywa (Abu Hayyah in Abu Hayyan's note); Jishumi says a nonconstruct reading is possible."}]}

{"id": "29:57/q08", "question": "What does returning to God mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:57/q08/p1", "position": "After death people are raised and brought to God's judgment for recompense according to deeds.", "reasons": "Bursevi derives turjaʿūn from rajʿ and glosses it 'you are returned'; he, Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Nasafi, Biqai and Alusi specify judgment and reward or punishment. {"id": "29:57/q09", "question": "How is the verb 'you are returned' read?", "turns_on": "The initial consonant changes direct address to third person, and vowel pattern changes passive return to active returning; the notes give differing transmitter attributions and contextual explanations.", "positions": [{"id": "29:57/q09/p1", "position": "It is read in direct address with tāʾ and passive voice: 'you are returned'.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid and Farisi name the other readers, including Hafs from Asim; Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and Nashr call it the majority reading. {"id": "29:57/q10", "question": "How does the reminder of death and return address migration?", "turns_on": "The sources emphasize either the impossibility of escaping death by staying home or the promised recompense after death; both serve the migration context.", "positions": [{"id": "29:57/q10/p1", "position": "Death is inevitable wherever one lives, so fear of death or livelihood should not delay migration and obedience.", "reasons": "Muqatil connects the warning to migrants without money or livelihood in Medina who trust God; Wahidi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Tabarsi and Ibn al-Jawzi say remaining among polytheists cannot prevent death.
